newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ALPINE SKIING-BAILEY HELPS OUT KATE PACE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-BAILEY HELPS OUT KATE PACE.

text.p: Having coaxed an Olympic gold medal out of Donovan Bailey, Mark Lindsay is hoping he can do the same thing with his own wife, former world downhill champion Kate Pace.

Lindsay, Bailey's personal chiropractor and physiotherapist, took his struggling wife to Austin, Texas to train with the 100-metres world record holder this year in an effort to help her rediscover the form that made her the 1994 champion.

"We actually train together, at the same time, with the same coaches," said Pace, who worked with Bailey's training group and his coach Dan Pfaff during the three months leading up to the Atlanta Olympics and again in the autumn.
"I work side-by-side with Donovan all day long. We just don't talk about training, we actually do the exact same stuff," she said.
Pace's hard work has not yet paid off in results. In the season's first two World Cup downhills, the 27 year-old Canadian placed a disappointing 18th and 21st.
She says she keeps in regular contact with Bailey, but the conversations of late have centered more on encouragement then technique.
"When we spoke to him last week he told me it takes a while to get used to all the new things that you learn.
"He told me he felt stiff after he first started training with this group and that it would be hard to let go and get into racing again."

Pace established herself as one of the sport's fiercest competitors in 1993 when, with her broken wrist wrapped in a cast and only one pole, she pushed out of the start hut and hurtled down a snowy course in Morioka, Japan to win the World championship downhill title.
The following season she looked poised to assume the mantle as the top woman's downhiller after winning the season opening downhill in Tignes, France.
It was the first and only World Cup win of her 10-year career and she finished the season second in downhill rankings to German Katja Seizinger.
In the seasons since, a string of nagging injuries have slowed Pace, although she did mount a valiant defence of her World title with a fourth place in Sierra Nevada this year.
"When I work as hard as I have, I expect results," said Pace, who expects to retire after next season's Nagano Olympics.
"I think right now I'm in a transition period, trying to put that quickness through my skis. Sometimes it's tough but I just have to be patient and believe it's going to come.
"All that hard work has to pay off sometime."
Pace's new training regime, co-ordinated by her husband who travels with her on the World Cup circuit as the Canadian team's physio and start coach, is a radical departure from her old regimen.
In past years, Pace would often train alone, taping inspiration messages to the handle bars of her mountain bike as she rode around the forests of her home in North Bay, Ontario.
"I don't bike as much as I use to," said Pace, who met her husband at the Lillehammer Olympics. "My coach has put me back on the ground.
"He wants me to have contact with my feet and the ground.
"Sometimes as an athlete you get into a rut with the same programme, the same trainers, doing the same thing for 10 years.
"I joined the old programme when I was 16 and things can get a bit monotonous. It wasn't a challegne anymore.
"When I started working with track athletes, it's something new every day and it's a challenge."
Whatever happens this season, Pace will be back to training with Bailey in the spring as he prepares for his 150-metre showdown with Michael Johnson in May.
"If nothing else," says Pace. "I know I'll always be faster than Donovan on skis."
